report:
**Conclusion:** The broad claim that *food-grade wax coatings on apples cause cancer* is not supported by credible evidence. It likely conflates the edible coating with other issues, such as pesticide residues or non-food-grade products.

Apples naturally have a waxy cuticle. Commercial washing can remove it, so producers may apply a replacement edible coating to reduce water loss and preserve quality. Common food-grade materials include carnauba wax (plant-derived), shellac, and similar approved glazing agents. [McGill Office for Science and Society](https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/you-asked/why-do-they-spray-wax-apples-0)

For example, U.S. food regulations list carnauba wax as a direct food substance affirmed as “generally recognized as safe” (GRAS), with specified food-use conditions. This is not a guarantee of zero risk under every hypothetical exposure, but it means the FDA recognizes safety for intended dietary use—not that it is a known carcinogen. [eCFR, 21 CFR §184.1978](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-184/subpart-B/section-184.1978)

International toxicology review also evaluated carnauba wax, including animal dietary studies, in its food-additive assessment; it does not identify cancer as an established effect at permitted food exposures. [WHO/JECFA toxicological monograph](https://inchem.org/documents/jecfa/jecmono/v30je13.htm)

**Important nuance:** “Food-grade wax” is a category, not a complete ingredient label. Safety depends on the specific approved formulation and dose. It is reasonable to wash apples under running water for general hygiene and to reduce surface residues, but there is no good evidence that eating approved wax-coated apples causes cancer.
